Three Counties to Vote on $2.4 Billion Transit Bond

By Dana Whitfield, October 2, 2026

Voters in three counties will decide in November whether to approve a $2.4 billion transit bond, the largest such measure in the region’s history. The money would pay for two new rail lines, faster buses, and repairs to stations that have not been updated since the 1980s.

Supporters, including most of the region’s mayors, say the bond is the only realistic way to cut traffic on the main highway, which carries twice the vehicles it was designed for. Opponents argue that property owners will carry most of the cost, and that ridership has not fully recovered since 2020.

The measure needs a two-thirds majority to pass. A poll by a local university in September found 61 percent support, short of the threshold, though about one in five voters said they were still undecided. You can read the full ballot text in our explainer below or on the county elections site.

Transit officials say construction would begin in 2028 and finish in stages over twelve years. The first part, an express bus corridor between the airport and downtown, could open within three years of the vote, according to the agency’s timeline.

What the ballot says

The measure would authorize the regional authority to issue bonds, repaid through a property tax of roughly $19 per $100,000 of assessed value. An independent oversight committee would review spending each year, and its reports would be posted online.

Critics have also questioned the project list, pointing out that one county would receive less than a fifth of the money, despite making up nearly a third of the population. The authority says the list reflects where current ridership is highest.
